questions.q: Which of the following is a mathematical statement? (a) "Please open the window." (b) "The sum of interior angles of a triangle is 180°." (c) "How beautiful the flower is!" (d) "x is an even number."
questions.a: (b) "The sum of interior angles of a triangle is 180°." This is a declarative sentence with a definite truth value (true). (a) is a command, (c) is an exclamation, (d) is an open sentence whose truth depends on the value of x. A wrong answer reveals the student cannot distinguish between sentences that have a fixed truth value and those that do not.

questions.q: Explain why "The square of a real number is always non-negative" is a statement, but "The square of a real number is always positive" is also a statement (though false). Why is "This sentence is false" not considered a mathematical statement?
questions.a: Both sentences are declarative and have a definite truth value: the first is true, the second is false. "This sentence is false" is a paradox (liar paradox) – it cannot be consistently assigned a truth value (if true then false, if false then true). A wrong answer indicates the student confuses falsity with non-statement status or fails to recognize self-referential paradoxes as excluded from mathematical statements.

questions.q:
Determine whether each is a statement. If yes, give its truth value.
(i) "All prime numbers are odd."
(ii) "There exists a real number x such that x² = -1."
(iii) "Solve the equation 2x + 3 = 7."
(iv) "The number π is rational."
questions.a: (i) Statement, false (2 is prime and even). (ii) Statement, false (no real number squares to -1). (iii) Not a statement (imperative/command). (iv) Statement, false (π is irrational). A wrong answer on (i) or (ii) shows the student thinks a false sentence is not a statement; on (iii) shows confusion between commands and assertions; on (iv) shows lack of knowledge about π but that doesn't affect statement classification.

questions.q: Consider the sentences: P: "n + 5 = 10" and Q: "There exists an integer n such that n + 5 = 10." Which is a statement? Why does adding a quantifier change the status?
questions.a: Q is a statement (true, n=5 works). P is not a statement because its truth depends on the free variable n. Quantifiers bind variables, removing ambiguity and yielding a definite truth value. A wrong answer reveals the student does not understand the role of free variables vs. quantified variables in determining statementhood.

questions.q: A student claims: "Since 'x > 5' is not a statement, 'For all real x, x > 5' is also not a statement because it still contains x." Evaluate this claim and correct the error.
questions.a: The claim is incorrect. "For all real x, x > 5" is a statement (it is false). The universal quantifier "for all" binds the variable x, making the sentence a complete assertion with a definite truth value. The student's error is not recognizing that quantifiers eliminate the dependency on a free variable. A wrong evaluation shows the student conflates the presence of a variable letter with the presence of a free variable.

questions.q: Create your own example of a sentence that looks like a statement but is not, due to a hidden ambiguity or subjectivity. Explain why it fails the definition.
questions.a: Example: "This triangle is large." It fails because "large" is subjective and context-dependent; there is no objective criterion to assign a definite truth value. A poor answer would give a sentence that is clearly a command or question, missing the nuance of apparent declarative sentences that lack objective truth conditions.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A mathematical statement is a declarative sentence that is either true or false, but not both ______.
Fill in the blank: Imagine your friend says: "The square of any integer is always ______." You wonder: Is this a sentence we can definitively label as true or false?
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can correctly classify any given sentence as a statement or non-statement, justify the classification by referencing the requirement of a definite truth value, and determine the truth value of simple mathematical statements.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine your friend says: "The square of any integer is always positive." You wonder: Is this a sentence we can ______ label as true or false?
